BiblicalUsage: Woe is me appears once, in the first song of ascents: Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar, and the psalmist goes on to say, My soul hath long dwelt with him that hateth peace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the psalmist's woe is the prayer of the exile: woe is me that I sojourn in Mesech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar, and God heard it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
